In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the chlorosomal bacteriochlorophyls are organized in aggregates with a radius of curvature of approximately 2.4-3.2 nm.
the structure of the aggregates in the chlorosomes of Chlorobaculum is a mixture of two types of curved structures, one with a curvature radius of ∼20 nm, the other one with a radius of ∼30 nm.
the chlorosomes consist of bacteriochloropyll aggregates that have a curved, but not a flat, structure.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have been able to determine the structural parameters of the bacteriochloryl aggregates that are responsible for the light harvesting function of chlorosomes.
chlorosomes are not only the most efficient light harvesting systems in photosynthetic organisms but also the most efficient self-assembling systems in nature.
we show that chlorosomes are not a single, but a mixture of several types of aggregates.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a detailed structural characterization of chlorosomes requires the analysis of individual particles and a combination of complementary experimental and theoretical techniques.

a combination of single-molecule spectroscopy with complementary methods can provide detailed structural information on complex assemblies, such as light harvesting complexes, even if they are not amenable to structural studies by conventional means.
a combination of single-particle spectroscopy with cryo-electron tomography is a powerful approach to study the structure and function of light-harvest- ing assemblies in photosynthetic membranes.
